data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's causal mechanism — that expert intuition is 'compressed experience' enabling rapid pattern recognition of outliers — provides no way to distinguish genuine reliability from luck within a single evaluation. The mechanism predicts the expert catches anomalies 'outside the checklist's predefined scope,' but on a task with objectively verifiable outcomes and only one evaluation round, any correct expert judgment on an out-of-scope item is observationally indistinguishable from a lucky guess. The problem explicitly demands evidence that separates real reliability from mere compliance that happens to track the right answer; SRC_002 offers no such evidentiary criterion. Worse, its mechanism actively undermines the required distinction: if the expert's advantage lies in detecting unchecklisted anomalies, and the evaluation only records right/wrong outcomes (not whether the right answer came from checklist-following or anomaly-spotting), then a single evaluation cannot attribute the expert's success to the cited mechanism rather than chance.
